Issued at 123 PM CDT Sat Aug 1 2026

Latest RAP analysis and satellite/radar imagery early this 
afternoon show a closed low pressure system spinning across 
central Illinois and southern Indiana. Light rain on the northern 
periphery of this feature has nearly exited east-central 
Wisconsin, leaving behind extensive cloud cover over southern 
counties. Farther north across north-central to far northeast 
Wisconsin, visible satellite depicts an expanding field of fair 
weather cumulus developing within an axis of 500 to 1000 J/kg 
of surface based instability. Over the next 36 to 48 hours, the 
central Illinois surface low will track slowly east- southeastward
toward the Ohio Valley, allowing high pressure over Ontario and 
the Upper Lakes to build southward into the western Great Lakes 
region.

As convective temperatures are approached this afternoon (around 
2 PM to 3 PM), widely scattered showers and isolated thunderstorms
are expected to initiate across north-central and northeast 
Wisconsin. Low-level surface convergence is relatively weak, but 
mesoanalysis indicates sufficient destabilization to support 
pulse-type convective updrafts. CAMS guidance indicates the 
highest probability for shower and storm activity will extend 
along a corridor from Marinette County southwest through Wood and 
Waushara Counties, with some CAMS tracking scattered activity into
the Fox Valley between 6 PM and 8 PM. Model forecast soundings 
exhibit shallow inverted-V profiles in the lowest levels, which 
will support localized wind gusts of 25 to 30 mph and brief 
visibility reductions under stronger showers. Convection should 
quickly wane mid to late evening with the loss of diurnal heating 
and the departure of the surface low to the southeast.

Attention then turns to cloud cover and temperature trends 
overnight into Sunday, as well as marine impacts. As the surface 
low pulls further away into the Ohio Valley, a tightening pressure
gradient and a longer fetch of northeast winds across Lake 
Michigan will push a surge of low stratus into northeastern and 
central Wisconsin late tonight into early Sunday morning. These 
low ceilings are expected to gradually lift into a 
stratocumulus/cumulus field by late Sunday morning as diurnal 
heating and dry air advection take hold. Skies should clear from 
north to south Sunday afternoon as strong surface high pressure 
builds south out of Ontario. High temperatures on Sunday will be 
somewhat suppressed by the low clouds and onshore flow, ranging 
from the mid 70s near Lake Michigan to near 80 degrees across 
central Wisconsin.

High pressure will center over the western Great Lakes Sunday 
night through Monday night, bringing a period of quiet and 
pleasant weather with near-normal temperatures and comfortable 
humidity. Highs on Monday will reach the upper 70s to mid 80s 
under mostly sunny skies. The next weather maker approaches 
Tuesday as a shortwave trough and associated surface cold front 
track eastward across the Upper Midwest. Convective parameters 
ahead of the boundary appear modest, with MUCAPE values peaking 
around 500 to 1000 J/kg and deep-layer shear around 25 to 30 
knots. This combination suggests a minimal threat for organized 
severe weather. However, precipitable water values rising to 120 
to 130 percent of normal alongside deep-layer flow aligned 
parallel to the surface frontal boundary could promote localized 
training of showers and storms, presenting a low risk for 
localized heavy rainfall.

Most global ensemble guidance rapidly pushes the cold front east
of the area by Wednesday morning, though lingering light rain 
showers cannot be ruled out over northeast Wisconsin early 
Wednesday. A notable outlier in deterministic guidance (GFS) holds
the front up and delays its eastern progression, maintaining 
heavy rainfall potential into Wednesday, but this solution lacks 
support from ensemble cluster means. High pressure builds back 
into the Upper Mississippi Valley behind the front for Wednesday 
and Thursday, returning dry weather and seasonal conditions. The 
next upper-level shortwave and cold front will bring the next 
opportunity for showers and thunderstorms toward next Friday into 
Saturday. Temperatures throughout the 7-day period will remain 
right around seasonal averages, with daily highs in the mid 70s to
mid 80s and overnight lows in the upper 40s to low 60s.
